### Question 1

Sensitivity asks exactly one question: out of the people who genuinely have the condition, what fraction does the test flag? Every person in this study was already confirmed sick by a reference standard, so the whole group of 100 is the denominator, and the 90 who tested positive are the numerator: 90/100 = 0.9. Nobody healthy was tested here, which is why this number cannot be specificity or a predictive value; those need information about disease-free people or about the full set of positive results.

### Question 2

Specificity is the mirror image of sensitivity: among people who are genuinely free of the condition, what fraction does the test correctly leave alone? The disease-free group has 250 people, and 225 of them got the correct negative result, so specificity is 225/250 = 0.9. The remaining 25 were false positives. Notice that the 60 diseased people never enter this calculation at all — mixing the two groups into one denominator is the most common error here.

### Question 3

Risk is a probability expressed as cases divided by everyone who could have become a case. Here 100 of the 400 people followed developed the outcome, so the risk is 100/400 = 0.25, or 25 per 100 people in a year. The word 'absolute' signals that the number stands alone with nothing to compare it against. Odds are a different construction — cases divided by non-cases, 100/300 = 0.33 — and ratios or differences of risk cannot exist until a second group is introduced.

### Question 4

Relative risk answers 'how many times as likely,' so it is a division problem, and the inputs must be risks rather than counts because the groups are different sizes. The exposed risk is 15/300 = 0.05; the unexposed risk is 5/500 = 0.01. Dividing gives 5, so exposure is associated with five times the risk. Subtracting instead gives 0.04, which is also meaningful but answers 'how much more,' not 'how many times more' — and comparing the raw counts 15 and 5 quietly assumes the two groups were the same size, which they were not.

### Question 5

Work with a concrete cohort first. Treating 100 people drops the number of events from 30 to 20, so those 100 treatments prevented 10 events — about 10 people treated per event prevented. The formula is the same arithmetic in compressed form: take the difference in risk, 0.3 minus 0.2 = 0.1, and invert it to get 10. A smaller number needed to treat means more benefit per person treated, and the number balloons when the risk difference is tiny.

### Question 6

Sensitivity 0.92 means that of every 100 people who truly have the condition, the test flags 92. The remaining 8 are missed — they are the false negatives — so the false-negative rate is 1 - 0.92 = 0.08. The tempting answer 0.15 is the leftover from specificity, but that leftover lives in a different population entirely: it counts healthy people who get an incorrect positive result, not sick people who get missed.

### Question 7

Picture the two groups as overlapping distributions of test values, with the cutoff as a movable line. Slide the line down and everything to its right is called positive, so more diseased results cross into positive territory (sensitivity up) and more disease-free results do too (specificity down). The data confirm the second half: correct negatives fell from 180/200 = 0.9 to 160/200 = 0.8. One line governs both groups, which is why you cannot gain on one measure without giving up ground on the other.

### Question 8

Sensitivity runs forward from disease to test result: given that you are sick, how often is the test positive? Positive predictive value runs backward from result to disease: given a positive test, how often is the person sick? In this cohort 180 people tested positive, and only 90 of them are true cases, so 90/180 = 0.5. The reason the backward question gives a much worse answer is that 900 disease-free people, each with a 10% chance of a false positive, generate 90 false alarms that dilute the 90 real detections.

### Question 9

The test did not get worse; the population changed. Of 10,000 people, 100 are diseased and 9,900 are not. A sensitivity of 0.9 yields 90 true positives from the small diseased group, while a 10% false-positive rate applied to 9,900 disease-free people yields 990 false positives. So 1,080 people get a positive result and only 90 are real: 90/1,080 = 0.08. Flip the question around and the news is good: 8,920 people test negative and only 10 of them are actually sick, so a negative result is right about 99.9% of the time. When a disease is rare, 'you are clear' becomes easier to believe and 'you are positive' becomes harder to believe.

### Question 10

Sequential testing splits the job in two: a wide first net, then a narrow second one. Missed cases are the costly error at stage one, because a person told they are negative goes home and is never checked again, while a false positive simply proceeds to the confirmatory test. Count the misses using the complement of sensitivity: Test A misses 2% of 500, or 10 people; Test B misses 20% of 500, or 100 people. Specificity tells you how much unnecessary follow-up you will pay for, not how many cases slip through.

### Question 11

Fill in the four cells before dividing anything. Of the 80 diseased people, the test catches 75%, so 60 are true positives and the other 20 are false negatives. Of the 320 disease-free people, 95% are correctly cleared, giving 304 true negatives. Now count everyone who received a negative result: 304 + 20 = 324, of whom 304 are genuinely disease-free, so 304/324 = 0.94. Specificity asked 'given healthy, how often negative'; this asks the reverse, 'given a negative result, how often healthy' — and the answer is reassuring here mainly because most of the population is disease-free to begin with.

### Question 12

Always ask 'half of what?' Half of a large risk is a large gain; half of 4 in 1,000 is 2 in 1,000. Treating 1,000 people therefore prevents 2 events, which works out to roughly 500 people treated per event prevented — the reciprocal of the 0.002 risk difference. Watch your decimal places when you invert: 1 divided by 0.002 is 500, while 1 divided by 0.2 is only 5, so losing two zeros makes the treatment look a hundred times more powerful than it is. The relative figure of 50% is not wrong, it is just scale-free: it tells you the proportion of baseline risk removed but nothing about how large that baseline was.
